health.title: Health check (no database)
health.description: Returns a constant JSON object without touching PostgreSQL.
health.why: Baseline: the ceiling of Express itself. Anything slower than this is cost added by the database or by our own code.
health.expect: Highest throughput of all targets; the API core hits 100 % CPU before anything else fails.

event-by-id.title: Event by id
event-by-id.description: Fetches one random event (id 1–1000) through its primary key index.
event-by-id.why: The cheapest realistic DB read, used for the main scaling experiment (E1).
event-by-id.expect: Latency flat in the low milliseconds until the API core saturates; then p95/p99 shoot up and throughput stops following the offered rate.

events-page.title: Paginated event list
events-page.cost: 2 queries: ORDER BY + OFFSET page, COUNT(*)
events-page.description: Random page 1–50 of 20 events, plus the total count.
events-page.why: Typical list endpoint: two queries per request and a bigger JSON response (more serialization work for Node).
events-page.expect: Knee at a lower rate than event-by-id; more CPU per request in both API and DB.

events-category.title: Events filtered by category
events-category.description: Random category out of 20; uses the category_id index.
events-category.why: Shows the cost of a filter + join compared with a plain primary-key lookup.
events-category.expect: Similar to the paginated list; the index keeps the database side cheap.

events-search.title: Text search (ILIKE)
events-search.cost: Sequential scan over all event texts
events-search.description: ILIKE '%word%' over titles and descriptions. No B-tree index can serve this, so PostgreSQL reads every row.
events-search.why: Database-bound endpoint: the bottleneck should move from the API to PostgreSQL.
events-search.expect: DB CPU rises much faster than for other reads; the pool wait count grows as queries take longer.

event-registrations.title: Registrations of an event
event-registrations.cost: JOIN registrations × users, ~50 rows of JSON
event-registrations.description: All registrations of a random event, each joined with its user.
event-registrations.why: Large response body: JSON.stringify of ~50 rows blocks the single Node event loop.
event-registrations.expect: Event-loop lag and API CPU climb earlier than for small responses.

category-stats.title: Category statistics (aggregate)
category-stats.description: Counts registrations per category: a reporting query that touches the whole registrations table.
category-stats.why: The heaviest read: shows what happens when every request is an analytical query.
category-stats.expect: Lowest sustainable rate; PostgreSQL is the bottleneck and requests queue in the pg pool.

create-event.title: Create event
create-event.description: Inserts a new event with random data.
create-event.why: Simplest write: every commit must be flushed to the write-ahead log (fsync), which reads never pay.
create-event.expect: Slower than reads at the same rate; DB CPU and IO dominate.

register.title: Register for an event
register.description: Random user (1–10 000) registers for a random event (1–1000). 409 (already registered / full) is an expected business answer, not an error.
register.why: The core business operation: a multi-statement transaction holding a pooled connection for its whole duration.
register.expect: Highest per-request cost of the normal endpoints; pool waiting grows first.

mix-100-0.title: Mix 100 % read / 0 % write
mix-100-0.description: Every iteration is one of: event by id, paginated list, category filter.
mix-100-0.why: Reference point for the read/write mix experiment (E3).
mix-100-0.expect: Lowest latency in the mix series.

mix-80-20.title: Mix 80 % read / 20 % write
mix-80-20.description: Typical web-shop-like ratio: mostly browsing, some registrations.

mix-50-50.title: Mix 50 % read / 50 % write
mix-50-50.description: Half of all requests are registrations.
mix-50-50.expect: Clearly higher DB load and latency.

mix-20-80.title: Mix 20 % read / 80 % write
mix-20-80.description: Mostly registrations, like the minute registration opens.

mix-0-100.title: Mix 0 % read / 100 % write
mix-0-100.expect: Highest latency and DB CPU in the mix series.

hot-event-rush.title: Hot-event rush (contention)
hot-event-rush.cost: All transactions lock the SAME row
hot-event-rush.description: setup() creates one event with 500 seats; every request tries to register a random user for that one event. The first 500 succeed, the rest get 409 'full'.
hot-event-rush.why: Row-lock contention: requests wait for each other inside PostgreSQL. Also a correctness test: registrations must never exceed capacity.
hot-event-rush.expect: Latency grows with rate even at modest load because transactions serialize on one row; registered_count ends exactly at 500.

smoke.title: Smoke
smoke.description: 1 virtual user, one request every 0.1 s (~10 req/s).
smoke.why: Sanity check that the endpoint works and the script is correct before a real test. Not a measurement.

constant.title: Constant rate (average load)
constant.description: Exactly RATE new requests start every second for DURATION, no matter how slow the API gets (open model).
constant.why: The measurement profile. Holding the offered load constant lets us compare levels; if the API cannot keep up, k6 reports dropped iterations instead of silently slowing down (avoids coordinated omission).

stress.title: Stress (ramp up)
stress.description: Rate grows linearly from 1 to RATE over DURATION.
stress.why: Shows the whole latency-vs-load curve in one run and roughly where degradation starts, so you know which constant levels to measure.

spike.title: Spike
spike.description: Quiet base load (5 % of RATE), a jump to RATE in 5 s, held for DURATION, then back down to base.
spike.why: Simulates the moment registrations open. Shows whether the API survives a sudden burst and how fast latency recovers afterwards.

soak.title: Soak (endurance)
soak.description: Moderate constant load for a long time.
soak.why: Finds problems that only appear over time: memory leaks (RSS keeps growing), connection leaks, slow drift in latency.

breakpoint.title: Breakpoint
breakpoint.description: Keeps ramping towards RATE and aborts automatically when p95 > 1 s, more than 5 % of requests fail, or k6 has to drop iterations because responses are too slow.
breakpoint.why: Finds the maximum rate the system can handle; the rate at the moment of abort is the breaking point.

experiments.title: Scaling: latency vs request rate (main experiment)
experiments.question: How does increasing the request rate affect latency, throughput, CPU and memory, and at what rate does performance degrade significantly?
experiments.hypothesis: Latency stays flat while the single API core has spare capacity; past a knee, p95/p99 rise sharply, achieved throughput stops following the offered rate and errors appear.
experiments.description: GET /api/events/:id at increasing constant rates. Each level is a separate run with a fresh API and DB. The levels go past the 10–1000 req/s from the original plan because a pilot showed one pinned M3 core serves ~5000 req/s for this endpoint.

experiments.title: Endpoint comparison at equal load
experiments.question: How much does the kind of work an endpoint does change its behaviour at the same request rate?
experiments.hypothesis: Endpoints with heavier queries or larger responses show higher latency and saturate a different resource (API CPU vs DB CPU).
experiments.description: All read endpoints at the same constant rate.

experiments.title: Read/write mix at equal total load
experiments.question: How does the share of write requests affect performance at the same total rate?
experiments.hypothesis: Latency and DB CPU grow with the write share, because writes hold transactions and flush the WAL.
experiments.description: Mixes from 100 % read to 100 % write at the same constant rate.

experiments.title: Spike: registrations open
experiments.question: Does the API survive a sudden burst and how fast does it recover?
experiments.hypothesis: Short latency peak during the jump, recovery within seconds once the spike ends.
experiments.description: 80/20 mix with a sudden jump to the peak rate.

experiments.title: Hot-event contention
experiments.question: How does lock contention on a single row affect latency as the rate grows?
experiments.hypothesis: Latency grows faster than for spread-out registrations because transactions wait on the same row lock; capacity is never exceeded.
experiments.description: Everyone registers for the same event at increasing rates.

experiments.title: Breaking points
experiments.question: What is the maximum sustainable rate of each type of endpoint?
experiments.description: Breakpoint ramp per endpoint until it breaks. The highest per-second rate the API actually served (api_rps_max) is the breaking point.
